title: Project Initiation: Business Case & Charter
sequence: the first project topic. Initiating authorizes the project or phase; Planning (Topics 14–23) elaborates it.

header.html: Process Task 1 Develop an integrated project management plan and plan delivery (assess project needs, complexity and magnitude; recommend the approach; determine critical information requirements) and Task 3 Help ensure value-based delivery (identify value components, examine business value). Also Business Environment Task 1 (success metrics, governance structure) and People Task 1 (shared vision) at the start of a project or phase.

toc.title: The Initiate Project or Phase Process
Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

html:
1The Initiating Focus Area

Initiating = the processes, practices or actions that define a new project or a new phase, often including formal authorization to start.

Aspect Detail
Purpose Align stakeholder expectations with the project's purpose; inform stakeholders of scope and objectives; align key stakeholders; discuss how their participation helps meet their expectations
What gets done Define initial scope; commit initial financial resources; identify stakeholders who will interact with and influence the outcome; assign project management roles
Typical artifacts Project charter, stakeholder register
Key benefit Projects are authorized only when aligned with the organization's strategic objectives, with the business case, benefits and stakeholders considered from the start
Who does it In some organizations the PM helps develop the business case and benefits; elsewhere a broader PM team helps write the charter; others have the sponsor, PMO, portfolio steering committee or another stakeholder group do the preliminary work
Sponsor's part The sponsor supplies the minimum information necessary for the PM to start. Involving sponsors, customers and other stakeholders at initiation builds a shared understanding of success criteria and increases alignment on deliverables and satisfaction

Initiating happens once or at certain points in the life cycle: at project start, and again for each phase (a phase can be initiated with a gate or a re-validation).

Why projects are authorized (Standard §1.3.2.1): meeting regulatory, legal or social requirements; satisfying stakeholder requests or needs; implementing or changing business or technology strategies; creating, improving or fixing products, processes, organizations or services. Every project should link to strategic objectives and business value.

2Business Documents

Business documents (the business case and the benefits management plan) generally originate outside the project and are inputs to it. Both are developed before the project, referenced after it ends, and reviewed periodically, so they are business documents, not project documents or parts of the project management plan. In some organizations they are maintained at program level.

2.1 Business case

Aspect Detail
Definition A documented economic feasibility study used to establish the validity of the benefits to be delivered by a portfolio component, program or project; a basis for authorizing further project management activity
Content The objectives and reasons for initiation: costs, benefits, how value will be created, and project success criteria
Uses May be used before initiation and may result in a go/no-go decision; helps measure success at the end against objectives; used throughout the life cycle
Accountability The project sponsor is generally accountable for developing and maintaining it. The project manager recommends and oversees so the success measures in the business case, project management plan, charter and benefits management plan stay aligned with each other and with organizational goals
Precursor A needs assessment feeds the business case and the benefits management plan Beyond PMBOK 8some courses call the high-level "business needs" document the prerequisite of a formal business case

2.2 Benefits management plan

The documented explanation of the processes for creating, maximizing and sustaining benefits: how and when benefits will be delivered and the mechanisms to measure them. A project benefit is an outcome of actions, behaviors, products, services or results that provides value to the sponsoring organization and the intended beneficiaries.

Element Meaning
Target benefits Expected tangible and intangible value; financial value may be expressed as net present value (NPV)
Strategic alignment Fit with the organization's business strategy
Timeframe for realizing benefits Short term, long term, ongoing, or by phase
Benefits owner Person accountable for monitoring, recording and reporting realized benefits over the timeframe
Metrics Direct and indirect measures of benefits realized
Assumptions Factors expected to be in place or evident
Risks Risks to realizing the benefits

It is developed and maintained iteratively, begins early in the life cycle with the target benefits, complements the business case, charter and project management plan, and describes how business value becomes part of ongoing operations with the metrics used to verify value and validate success. The PM works with the sponsor to keep the charter, project management plan and benefits management plan aligned (Topic 10).

2.3 Agreements

Any document or communication that defines the initial intentions of a project: a contract, service-level agreement (SLA), memorandum of understanding (MOU), letter of agreement, verbal agreement, purchase order, email, and so on. They may be simple or complex (a complex project may have several contracts at once or in sequence) and must comply with local, national and international contract law. In cross-corporate projects, contracts bind the organizations and charters inside each organization create internal agreements to meet the contractual obligations.

3The Initiate Project or Phase Process

Item Detail
Purpose Officially authorize the start of a project and grant the project manager the authority to allocate organizational resources to project activities by creating a project charter (or similar document); it establishes a direct link between the project, the business case and strategic goals and an official record of the organization's commitment
Inputs Business documents (business case, benefits management plan), agreements, enterprise environmental factors, organizational process assets
Tools and techniques Expert judgment; data gathering (brainstorming, focus groups, interviews); interpersonal and team skills (conflict management, facilitation, meeting management); meetings; responsibility assignment matrix (RAM); project canvas
Outputs Project charter; assumption log
Frequency Usually once, or at certain points in the life cycle depending on the approach (e.g., each phase)

Beyond PMBOK 8practice for the ECO enabler "assess project needs, complexity and magnitude" At initiation, the PM and sponsor ask: what is the need and expected value? How complex and large is the work (technology, stakeholders, regulation, uncertainty)? What approach (predictive, adaptive, hybrid) fits (Topic 03)? What constraints and assumptions exist? Who are the key stakeholders and who decides? This sets up the integrated plan (Topic 14).

Related tools

  • Project canvas: a one-page visual that outlines the project's key elements for quick shared understanding. Typical sections: purpose, objective, scope/requirements, scope/deliverables, project approval requirements (what is success, who decides, who approves), assumptions and constraints, milestones and phases, scope exclusions, resources, stakeholders, users, risks, team, lessons learned.
  • RAM / RACI: responsible, accountable, consulted, informed; clarifies roles (Topic 19).
  • Assumption log: records all assumptions and constraints throughout the life cycle. High-level constraints usually come from the business case into the charter; lower-level assumptions are generated through the project (technical specifications, estimates, activities, risks) and are updated or closed out.

4The Project Charter

Definition: a document issued by the project initiator or sponsor that formally authorizes the existence of a project and gives the PM the authority to apply organizational resources to project activities.

Point Detail
Role Forms a partnership between the performing and requesting organizations; the approved business case (or similar) justifies initiation and the expected value
Who writes it The sponsor or the project manager, in collaboration with the initiating entity; PM involvement helps the PM understand the purpose, objectives and expected benefits and allocate resources efficiently
Project manager Identified and assigned as early as possible: ideally during charter development and always before planning begins. The approved charter grants the PM the authority to support the project
Contents (Table 4-1) Project purpose; measurable objectives and success criteria; high-level requirements; high-level description, boundaries and key deliverables; overall project risk; summary milestone schedule; preapproved financial resources; key stakeholder list; project approval requirements (what constitutes success, who decides, who approves); project exit criteria (conditions to close or cancel the project or phase); assigned PM with responsibility and authority level; name and authority of the sponsor or authorizer
Changes Changes to the charter are approved by the sponsor/initiator (the sponsor approves the charter and any changes to it, Topic 13)

4.1 Charter vs project scope statement vs project management plan

Project charter Project scope statement Project management plan
Level High level Detailed description of scope components Integrated plan and baselines
Purpose Authorize the project and the PM; confirm purpose, objectives, high-level scope Common understanding of scope; baseline to judge whether requests are inside or outside the boundaries How the project will be executed, monitored, controlled and closed
Contains Elements above Scope description (progressively elaborated), deliverables, acceptance criteria, exclusions All subsidiary plans, baselines, approach, life cycle
Owner Sponsor/initiator Project team Project manager and team

The charter and scope statement can look redundant, but they differ in level of detail.

4.2 Charters in adaptive approaches

Charters are more flexible: from a minimal worksheet or concise vision statement to a moderately detailed document, giving "just enough structure" while allowing requirements and priorities to evolve. An adaptive charter typically answers a subset or all of: Why is the project being undertaken? Who will be engaged? What is it about? Where will it occur? When will it start and end? How will it be carried out? Who is the customer?

5Initiating in Practice

  1. Confirm authorization and authority. No charter (or equivalent) = no formal authority. If missing, work with the sponsor to get it issued before planning begins.
  2. Confirm the value case. Check the business case and benefits plan: objectives, success criteria, timeframe, benefits owner. Surface conflicting definitions of success before baselining.
  3. Identify stakeholders and engage the sponsor, customers and key stakeholders (Topic 13).
  4. Record assumptions and constraints (assumption log) and make hidden or conflicting expectations explicit.
  5. Choose the initial approach and life cycle (Topic 03) and note tailoring needs (Topic 05).
  6. Clarify governance: decision rights, escalation paths and thresholds, who approves trade-offs (Topic 12).
  7. Kick off with shared purpose, roles and working agreements; for each new phase, re-validate that the business case and priorities still hold.

6Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Charter Formal charter with measurable objectives, milestones, funds, exit criteria Lightweight charter, vision statement or project canvas Formal for committed/contractual aspects, light for the rest
Business case Authorizes the whole project; revalidated at phase gates Revisited as value is reprioritized each iteration or release; funding in time-boxed tranches Both
Initiation frequency Project start and each phase Initial vision and roadmap, then continuous refinement; release-level initiation Mixed
PM role Often drafts or helps draft the charter Product owner and team shape the vision; PM/scrum master facilitates alignment Shared

7Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. The charter authorizes the project and the PM. Planning begins after the charter; assign the PM as early as possible. A PM without a charter lacks formal authority to apply resources.
  2. Business case and benefits management plan are business documents. They exist before the project and are referenced after; the sponsor is accountable for the business case, while the PM keeps success measures aligned and recommends updates.
  3. Revalidate value, not just performance. If the business case changes (market, cost, regulation), take it to the sponsor before continuing.
  4. Charter ≠ scope statement ≠ plan. Charter = high-level authorization; scope statement = detailed scope with acceptance criteria and exclusions; plan = how to execute.
  5. Surface hidden assumptions and conflicting expectations early, and agree on them before baselining (assumption log).
  6. Decision rights belong in governance from the start. If trade-offs or spending limits have no owner, work with the sponsor to define them; do not infer or take them.
  7. Do not wait for perfect information. The sponsor provides the minimum needed; elaborate progressively with stakeholders.
  8. Different leaders, different definitions of success → bring them together to agree one statement of success; do not just record both.
  9. Contracts may initiate cross-organizational work; each organization still needs an internal charter to deliver the obligations.
  10. Phases are initiated too. Re-check the business case and readiness at each phase gate.
  11. Success criteria and exit criteria belong in the charter, so the team knows when to close or cancel.

8Exam Q&A

8.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1A project manager joins a project that is already under way and cannot find an approved charter. The sponsor says to just keep going. What should the project manager do first?

  • AAsk the sponsor to issue a charter that names the PM and grants authority
  • BAsk the project team to sign off a charter on the sponsor's behalf
  • CCarry on with the detailed planning and obtain the charter later
  • DWrite the charter personally and treat it as approved by default
Show the answer

Answer: A. A charter formally authorizes the project and gives the project manager the authority to apply resources, and the sponsor or initiator must issue it before planning continues. Planning without it, self-approving it or having the team approve it all lack that authority.

S2The project manager of a hybrid program is appointed after the charter is signed and finds that its summary milestone cannot be met with the approved resources. What should the project manager do?

  • AAsk the team to work overtime from the start so that the date can be kept
  • BPlan to the charter's milestone and mention the shortfall when it occurs
  • CRewrite the milestone in the project plan and leave the charter unchanged
  • DTake the evidence to the sponsor and request that the charter be revised
Show the answer

Answer: D. The sponsor approves the charter and any changes to it, so a conflict between the charter and a realistic plan goes to the sponsor with evidence, and the project manager should have a voice in the charter early. Hiding the gap, rewriting the plan alone or planning overtime from day one leaves the authorization inconsistent.

S3The sponsor of an adaptive product cannot yet describe detailed requirements and asks the project manager to start, but the project manager would prefer a full specification before the charter is issued. What is the best approach?

  • AHold the charter until stakeholders have signed off a complete specification
  • BWrite the detailed requirements alone from experience and present them as final
  • CIssue the charter with high-level requirements and elaborate them progressively
  • DAsk the sponsor to cancel initiation until the missing detail is available
Show the answer

Answer: C. The sponsor supplies the minimum information needed to start, and requirements are elaborated progressively with stakeholders. Waiting for a full specification, inventing one or pausing initiation delays authorization without reducing the uncertainty.

S4The business case forecasts an 8% revenue lift, the charter promises 10% and the benefits management plan targets 6%. What should the project manager do?

  • ALeave the figures as they are, since each document has a different purpose
  • BWork with the sponsor to align the three documents on one validated target
  • CUse the lowest figure so that the team can safely over-deliver
  • DUse the charter figure because it authorizes the project and the manager
Show the answer

Answer: B. The sponsor is accountable for the business case, while the project manager keeps the success measures in the plan, charter and benefits management plan aligned with one another. Picking one figure, choosing the safest or accepting the mismatch leaves stakeholders with conflicting targets.

S5The sponsor asks who is accountable for developing and maintaining the business case. What is correct?

  • AThe PMO, which approves every business case in the organization
  • BThe sponsor, with the project manager keeping success measures aligned
  • CThe project manager alone, because the plan is built from it
  • DThe project team, because it delivers the benefits it describes
Show the answer

Answer: B. The sponsor is generally accountable for developing and maintaining the business case, while the project manager recommends and keeps the success measures in the plan, charter and benefits management plan aligned.

S6A charter lists the purpose and high-level requirements but no exit criteria. Why does that matter?

  • AExit criteria belong only in the schedule and need no sponsor input
  • BExit criteria are needed only in adaptive projects with short iterations
  • CExit criteria say when to close or cancel the project or phase
  • DIt does not matter, since closing conditions are agreed at the end
Show the answer

Answer: C. Exit criteria are the conditions for closing or canceling a project or phase, so the team and sponsor know when they are met, and the charter should state them. They are not an end-stage detail, a schedule field or an adaptive-only concept.

S7A reviewer rejects a charter because it lacks a detailed deliverables list with acceptance criteria and exclusions. How should the project manager respond?

  • ADelete the high-level deliverables so that no detail is expected there
  • BMove the detail into the benefits management plan, because that document covers deliverables
  • CExpand the charter with the full detail so that the reviewer is satisfied
  • DExplain that the charter is high level and the detail belongs in the scope statement
Show the answer

Answer: D. The charter authorizes the project at a high level, while the project scope statement holds the detailed scope description, acceptance criteria and exclusions. Padding the charter, removing content or using the benefits plan mixes up the documents.

S8A start-up using an adaptive approach asks whether it needs a 20-page charter. What is the best advice?

  • ANo documents at all, since adaptive teams do not need authorization
  • BYes, because every project needs the same formal charter regardless of approach
  • CA concise vision statement or canvas answering why, who, what and when
  • DOnly a budget estimate, because everything else changes too quickly
Show the answer

Answer: C. Adaptive charters are flexible: a concise vision statement, worksheet or canvas that answers why, who, what, where, when, how and who the customer is gives just enough structure. A heavy charter, nothing or only a budget misses that balance.

S9Two companies deliver a system together under a contract. What is the role of project charters?

  • AEach organization's charter creates internal agreements to meet the contract
  • BOne shared charter replaces the contract between the two companies
  • CCharters are unnecessary because the contract already authorizes the work
  • DCharters are issued only by customers to the companies they hire
Show the answer

Answer: A. In cross-corporate projects the contract binds the organizations, and each organization's charter creates the internal agreements needed to meet the contractual obligations. A contract does not replace internal authorization.

S10At the start of the next phase of a hybrid program, the sponsor asks the project manager to restate what the phase will deliver and why. Which practice supports this?

  • ASkip the step, since the project as a whole has already been formally authorized
  • BInitiate the phase by confirming objectives, business case and resources
  • CAsk the sponsor to replace the project manager for this phase
  • DClose the current project and open a new one for the design work
Show the answer

Answer: B. Phases can be initiated and gated, so objectives, business case alignment and resources are reconfirmed at the start of each. Skipping the step, closing the project or replacing the manager does not provide that confirmation.

8.2 Recall Q&As

R1What does the Initiating Focus Area do?

Show the answer

Defines a new project or phase and usually obtains formal authorization; aligns stakeholder expectations, defines initial scope, commits initial funds, identifies stakeholders and assigns PM roles.

R2What are the business documents?

Show the answer

The business case and the benefits management plan.

R3What is a business case?

Show the answer

A documented economic feasibility study that establishes the validity of the benefits to be delivered; basis for authorization and go/no-go.

R4What does the benefits management plan contain?

Show the answer

Target benefits, strategic alignment, timeframe, benefits owner, metrics, assumptions, risks.

R5What does the Initiate Project or Phase process produce?

Show the answer

The project charter and the assumption log.

R6What does the charter give the project manager?

Show the answer

Formal authority to apply organizational resources to project activities.

R7When should the PM be assigned?

Show the answer

As early as possible, ideally during charter development and always before planning begins.

R8List five charter elements.

Show the answer

Purpose; measurable objectives and success criteria; high-level requirements; summary milestones; preapproved funds; key stakeholders; approval requirements; exit criteria; PM and sponsor authority.

R9How does the scope statement differ from the charter?

Show the answer

It is more detailed: scope description, deliverables, acceptance criteria, exclusions.

R10What is a project canvas?

Show the answer

A one-page visual outlining the key elements of the project for shared understanding.

R11What is an agreement?

Show the answer

Any document or communication defining initial intentions: contract, SLA, MOU, letter of agreement, verbal agreement, PO, email.

R12Who is accountable for the business case?

Show the answer

Generally the sponsor; the PM recommends and keeps success measures aligned.

9Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Initiating Authorizes a project or phase; links to strategy; identifies stakeholders and assigns PM roles
Business documents Business case + benefits management plan; exist before; referenced after; sponsor accountable
Business case Economic feasibility; objectives, costs, benefits, success criteria; go/no-go
Benefits plan Target benefits, alignment, timeframe, owner, metrics, assumptions, risks
Process outputs Project charter, assumption log
Charter Issued by sponsor/initiator; authorizes project and PM authority; high level
PM assignment As early as possible; before planning
Charter contents Purpose, objectives/success criteria, requirements, boundaries, risk, milestones, funds, stakeholders, approval, exit criteria, PM, sponsor
Charter vs scope statement High level vs detailed (deliverables, acceptance criteria, exclusions)
Adaptive charter Light: vision, canvas; why/who/what/where/when/how/customer
Agreements Contract, SLA, MOU, letter, PO, email
Revalidate Business case changes → sponsor; each phase re-checks
First-action pattern Confirm authorization, confirm value and success definition, surface assumptions, clarify decision rights
